multistep-energy-profiles-s1.title: A two-step reaction
multistep-energy-profiles-s1.text:
The energy profile for a reaction that happens in two elementary steps:

Step 1: A + B → C   Step 2: C → D

Reaction progress has no units.

multistep-energy-profiles-s2.title: Energies along a three-step reaction
multistep-energy-profiles-s2.text: A reaction happens in three elementary steps. The table lists the potential energy of each point along its energy profile, in order.

items.q: Where is the intermediate C on the profile?
options: In the valley between the two peaks, at 80 kJ/mol
At the first peak, at 140 kJ/mol
At the second peak, at 110 kJ/mol
At the right-hand plateau, at 20 kJ/mol

why.correct: An intermediate is a real species made in step 1 and used in step 2, so it sits in the local minimum between the two transition states.
options: Right: the valley between the steps.
The first peak is the transition state of step 1, not a species that can be isolated.
The second peak is the transition state of step 2.
The right-hand plateau is the product D.

items.q: What is the activation energy of step 2, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: you measured from the reactants (50). Step 2 starts at the intermediate (80 kJ/mol): 110 − 80.
Value: that is the energy of the second transition state. Subtract the level step 2 starts from.

why.correct: Step 2 starts at the intermediate (80 kJ/mol) and climbs to the second transition state (110 kJ/mol): Ea = 110 − 80 = 30 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which step is rate-determining, and what is the evidence?
options: Step 1: its barrier, 90 kJ/mol, is larger
Step 2: its transition state comes later in the reaction
Step 2: its barrier ends nearest to the products
Step 1: being first, it is the slowest by rule

why.correct: Step 1 climbs 140 − 50 = 90 kJ/mol; step 2 climbs 110 − 80 = 30 kJ/mol. The larger barrier means fewer successful collisions, so step 1 is slower and limits the rate.
options: Right: compares the two activation energies.
Position along the reaction coordinate does not decide which step is slower.
Where a step ends says nothing about its barrier.
The first step is not slowest by rule; here it is slowest because of its barrier.

items.q: What rate law does this profile predict for the overall reaction A + B → D?
options: rate = k[A][B]
rate = k[C]
rate = k[A][B][C]
rate = k[D]

why.correct: Step 1 (A + B → C) is the slow step and comes first, so its rate law is the overall rate law: rate = k[A][B].
options: Right: from the slow first step.
That is the rate law of the fast step, and C is an intermediate.
C is an intermediate and does not belong in the rate law.
D is a product.

items.q: What is the overall energy change for A + B → D, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: the products (20) are below the reactants (50), so energy is released and the change is negative.
Value: compare the products with the reactants, not with the intermediate: 20 − 50.

why.correct: Energy change = E(products) − E(reactants) = 20 − 50 = −30 kJ/mol. The intermediate and transition states do not affect it.

items.q: What is the activation energy of step 2, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: step 2 starts from intermediate 1 (20 kJ/mol), not from the reactants.
Value: that runs from transition state 2 down to intermediate 2. Step 2 climbs from intermediate 1 up to transition state 2.

why.correct: Step 2 goes from intermediate 1 (20 kJ/mol) up to transition state 2 (95 kJ/mol): Ea = 95 − 20 = 75 kJ/mol.

options: Step 1 (Ea = 45 kJ/mol)
Step 2 (Ea = 75 kJ/mol)
Step 3 (Ea = 50 kJ/mol)
Step 3, since it releases the most energy

why.correct: Barriers: step 1, 45 − 0 = 45; step 2, 95 − 20 = 75; step 3, 40 − (−10) = 50 kJ/mol. Step 2 has the largest barrier, and its transition state is also the highest point on the profile, so it is the slow step.
options: Step 1 has the smallest barrier.
Right: the largest barrier and the highest transition state.
Step 3's barrier is 50 kJ/mol, smaller than step 2's.
Releasing energy does not make a step slow; the barrier does.

items.q: How many intermediates does this mechanism have, and how many transition states?
options: 2 intermediates and 2 transition states
2 intermediates and 3 transition states
3 intermediates and 2 transition states
3 intermediates and 3 transition states

why.correct: Three elementary steps give three peaks (transition states) and two valleys between them (intermediates).
options: Each of the three steps has its own peak.
Right: n steps, n peaks, n − 1 valleys.
This swaps the counts: peaks are transition states.
The valleys sit between peaks, so there is one fewer of them.

items.q: What is the overall energy change of the reaction, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: the products are below the reactants, so the change is negative.
Value: you compared the products with intermediate 2 (−60 − (−10)). The overall change is products minus reactants: −60 − 0.

items.q: On a multistep energy profile, what does each peak represent?
options: The transition state of one elementary step
An intermediate that can be isolated
The products of the overall reaction
A point where no bonds are changing

why.correct: Each elementary step has its own barrier, so each peak is that step's transition state.
options: Right: one peak per step.
Intermediates are in the valleys, not at the peaks.
The products are the final plateau.
At a peak, bonds are partly broken and partly formed.

items.q: A two-step profile shows a deep valley below the reactant level (a very stable intermediate) and a second peak higher than the first. A student says, "Step 1 is first, so it must be the slow step." Which response is best?
options: Step 2 has the larger climb from its valley, so it is slower
The student is right; the first step is the slow one
Both steps are equally slow, since there are two peaks
The deep valley means the reaction does not happen

why.correct: The slow step is the one with the larger barrier measured from where that step starts. A deep valley followed by a high second peak makes step 2's climb the largest.
options: Right: compare barriers from each step's starting level.
Order in the mechanism does not decide speed; barrier height does.
Two peaks do not mean equal barriers.
A stable intermediate just means step 2 has a large climb; the reaction still goes.

items.q: For a two-step reaction, step 1 has Ea = 60 kJ/mol and step 2 has Ea = 25 kJ/mol. The reactants are at 0 kJ/mol and the intermediate at 35 kJ/mol. What is the energy of the second transition state?
options: 25 kJ/mol
35 kJ/mol
60 kJ/mol
85 kJ/mol

why.correct: Step 2 starts at the intermediate (35 kJ/mol) and climbs 25 kJ/mol: 35 + 25 = 60 kJ/mol. (The first transition state is also at 0 + 60 = 60 kJ/mol.)
options: That is the barrier of step 2, not the level of its peak.
That is the level of the intermediate.
Right: intermediate plus the step 2 barrier.
That adds both barriers but ignores that step 2 starts from the intermediate, not from step 1's peak.

items.q: A two-step reaction has a slow first step. Suppose step 2 were changed so its barrier became even smaller, with nothing else changed. Predict each effect.

variables.name: Overall rate
variables.why: Step 1 is still the slow step, so it still sets the rate.

variables.name: Overall energy change
variables.why: The reactant and product levels are unchanged.

variables.name: Energy of the intermediate
variables.why: The valley level is unchanged; only the second peak drops.

why.correct: Lowering a barrier that is not rate-determining leaves the overall rate, the overall energy change and the intermediate level unchanged.

items.q: A three-step reaction profile is drawn. How many valleys lie between the reactant and product plateaus?

why.correct: There is one valley between each pair of neighboring peaks: three peaks give two valleys, one for each intermediate.
options: One valley would mean two steps.
Right: two intermediates.
Three is the number of peaks.
Four would mean five steps.

items.q: Why is an intermediate on an energy profile drawn in a valley rather than at a peak?
options: It is a real, if short-lived, species that sits at a local minimum
It has more energy than both transition states around it
It forms after the reaction is complete
It is the same as the transition state

why.correct: An intermediate is a species with fully formed bonds that lasts long enough to collide again. That makes it a local minimum, lower than the transition states on either side.
options: Right: a local minimum between barriers.
It is lower in energy than the transition states on either side.
It forms and is used during the reaction.
A transition state is a peak; an intermediate is a valley.
